function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
I don’t have the ability to clone repositories, inspect their contents, or make commits on your behalf.  
What I can do is give you the exact files you’ll need to add to the **nodejs‑welcome** repository so that it’s ready for Docker, Kubernetes, and GitHub Actions.  

Below are:

| File | Purpose | Suggested content |
|------|---------|-------------------|
| `Dockerfile` | Build a container image for the Node.js app | See the snippet below |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deployment + Service definition | See the snippet below |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | GitHub Actions workflow that builds & pushes the image on pushes to `main` | See the snippet below |

> **Tip:** If you want to keep the Kubernetes manifests in a separate folder, create a `k8s/` directory (or whatever you prefer) and put the YAML there. The GitHub Actions workflow will reference that path.

---

## 1. Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` at the root of the repository with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Use an official Node runtime as a parent image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set metadata
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"
EXPOSE 3000

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install app dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Bundle app source
COPY . .

# Start the application
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> *Why this Dockerfile?*  
> - `node:18-alpine` is lightweight and contains only what you need.  
> - `npm ci` guarantees reproducible installs from `package-lock.json`.  
> - Exposing port `3000` matches the typical Express default; adjust if your app uses another port.

---

## 2. Kubernetes YAML

Create a directory called `k8s/` (or `deploy/`, etc.) and inside it create a file named `deployment.yaml` with the following content:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your registry/image
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> *Adjustments you might need:*  
> - Change `replicas` to the desired number of pods.  
> - Update the `image` field to point to the actual image you’ll publish (e.g., `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`).  
> - If you’re running in a cluster that doesn’t support `LoadBalancer`, switch to `NodePort` or `ClusterIP`.

---

## 3. GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a directory `.github/workflows/` (if it doesn’t exist) and inside it create a file named `ci.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write   # Needed to push to GHCR

    steps:
    - name: Checkout repository
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: ./Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> *What this does:*  
> 1. Checks out the repo.  
> 2. Sets up Docker Buildx for multi‑platform builds.  
> 3. Logs into GitHub Packages (`ghcr.io`) using the automatically supplied `GITHUB_TOKEN`.  
> 4. Builds the image from the `Dockerfile` and pushes it to `ghcr.io/<owner>/nodejs-welcome:latest`.

> **Important:**  
> - Make sure the repository has the `GHCR` scope enabled for the `GITHUB_TOKEN` (this is automatic for public repos).  
> - If you’re using a private registry other than GHCR, change the `registry`, `username`, and `password` fields accordingly.

---

## 4. Add, Commit, Push

Once you’ve added the three files above to your local clone of the repository, run:

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

That will trigger the GitHub Actions workflow, which will build the image and push it to the registry. After the push succeeds, you can apply the Kubernetes manifests:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
```

---

### Recap

| Step | What to do |
|------|------------|
| 1 | Clone the repo locally (`git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`). |
| 2 | Add the three files shown above. |
| 3 | Commit and push (`git add … && git commit … && git push`). |
| 4 | Verify the GitHub Actions run succeeded. |
| 5 | Deploy to your cluster (`kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml`). |

Feel free to tweak the values (image names, ports, replica counts, etc.) to match your environment. Let me know if you’d like help customizing any part!
